name: The Triplicate

stars.name: Sol Primus
stars.notes: Nearly identical to Sol; forms the inner binary pair with Sol Secundus at 0.8 AU separation

stars.name: Sol Secundus
stars.notes: Twin of Sol Primus; the inner pair completes mutual orbit every 210 days

stars.name: Sol Tertius
stars.notes: Orbits the inner pair at 42 AU, completing one circuit every 195 years. All three stars formed from the same molecular cloud fragment.

planets.name: Mimic
planets.notes: Tidally locked to the inner pair. Surface temperature swings wildly as the twin suns eclipse one another.

planets.name: Concordance
planets.notes: Habitable world with a double-sunned sky. Complex seasonal cycles created by the inner binary produce lush equatorial forests and polar deserts.

planets.name: Parallax
planets.notes: Second habitable world, slightly cooler. Known for its triple-shadow phenomenon when all three suns are visible.

planets.name: The Triplet
planets.notes: Massive gas giant in a circumbinary orbit around the inner pair. Its three largest moons are tidally heated and geologically active.

planets.name: Harmony
planets.notes: Outermost planet of the inner system. Stable despite the triple-star configuration due to precise orbital resonance.

planets.name: Tertius-I
planets.notes: Orbits Sol Tertius exclusively. Ice world with subsurface ocean heated by tidal interaction with Tertius.

planets.name: Tertius-II
planets.notes: Cold, airless rock orbiting Sol Tertius. Rich in rare earth elements.

planets.name: Tertius-III
planets.notes: Distant ice dwarf at the edge of Sol Tertius's influence. Mostly nitrogen ice with trace organics.

planets.name: Reverberation
planets.notes: Gas giant in a wide circum-trinary orbit, taking over 800 years to complete one circuit around the entire three-star system.

planets.name: Echo
planets.notes: Outermost body, technically orbiting the system barycenter. Highly elliptical orbit; some astronomers dispute whether it qualifies as a true planet.

anomalies.name: Triple Stellar Resonance
anomalies.notes: Three nearly identical G-type stars in a stable hierarchical triple configuration is extraordinarily rare. Statistical models predict fewer than one such system per galaxy. The mechanism that prevented mass divergence during formation remains unexplained.

anomalies.name: The Symmetry Zone
anomalies.notes: A region where the gravitational pull of Sol Primus and Sol Secundus perfectly cancel, creating a near-zero-g corridor that shifts with the binary orbit. Used as an anchorage by station engineers.

anomalies.name: Triple Shadow Meridian
anomalies.notes: When all three suns are above the horizon simultaneously—roughly 40 days per Parallax year—every object casts three distinct shadows in slightly different hues of gold. Cultural festivals mark this period.

asteroid_belts.name: The Interstitial Band
asteroid_belts.location: Between inner binary system and Sol Tertius orbit (8-15 AU)
asteroid_belts.notes: Gravitationally stirred debris that never coalesced due to perturbation from all three stars. Rich in primitive solar nebula material.

stations.name: Triplicate Station
stations.notes: Primary hub for the system's two inhabited worlds. Serves as trade nexus and governmental seat.

stations.name: The Fulcrum
stations.notes: Astrophysics research station studying the triple-star configuration. Maintains position through constant micro-corrections.

stations.name: Tertius Outpost
stations.notes: Rare earth element extraction facility supplying both inhabited worlds.

faction_control.notes: The two inhabited worlds formed a joint government early in colonization. Relations are cooperative, bound by shared wonder at their improbable home.

history: First observed in 2298 by the Meridian Deep Survey. The discovery of three nearly identical solar-type stars in stable triple configuration was initially dismissed as instrument error until confirmed by four independent observatories.

Colonized in 2372 after probes confirmed two habitable worlds. The colony ships carried a deliberate cultural mandate: the settlers would treat their improbable home as a shared inheritance, not a resource to be divided.

The Triple Shadow Festival on Parallax, celebrated since 2391, has become one of the most famous cultural events in the sector, drawing tourists from across the Meridian Expanse during the forty-day convergence.
description: The Triplicate is a statistical impossibility made real—three G5V stars, each within 2% of solar mass, locked in a stable hierarchical triple. Sol Primus and Sol Secundus orbit one another tightly while Sol Tertius circles the pair at a distance of 42 AU. The configuration should not exist; stellar formation models cannot account for three stars condensing from the same cloud fragment with such precise mass parity. Ten planets orbit in various configurations—some circling the inner pair, some bound to Tertius alone, and two audacious bodies tracing wide paths around all three stars together.

Two habitable worlds make the improbability useful. Concordance orbits the inner binary in the habitable zone, its sky dominated by twin suns that eclipse one another in complex patterns, driving intricate seasons. Parallax sits farther out but within the zone where warmth from the pair sustains liquid water. Forty days each year, Sol Tertius rises above Parallax's horizon to join its siblings, and every object on the surface casts three golden shadows at slightly different angles—a phenomenon that has become the centerpiece of the planet's cultural identity.

The Triplicate draws scientists as much as settlers. The Fulcrum research station hangs at the inner binary's barycenter, studying a gravitational configuration that defies formation theory. Proposals range from the mundane—a spectacularly unlikely but natural coincidence—to the provocative: that some intelligence tuned the system's initial conditions. The Triplicate Concordat governs both worlds with a cooperative ethos born from shared awe, and the system's moderate traffic reflects a healthy mix of trade, tourism, and academic pilgrimage. In a galaxy of dead rocks and hostile radiation, The Triplicate is a reminder that the universe occasionally produces something beautiful for no apparent reason.
